hearing (p. 61–80)

Pages 61–80 (20 pages)
Abhidhamma hearing (p. 61–80) p. 61

“The condition for right mindfulness is intellectual understanding of what nama and rūpa are”

hearing less attachment, understanding sati (mindfulness) right understanding and reading anger, ignorance about nāma and rūpa, what has been heard: of one reality, for grows, one moment more patience, time and again realities through six one moment, when conditioning the next loving-kindness and doors conditions are there compassion

none of these moments is made by a self; each arises because the one before it was there “Even one moment of mindfulness is valuable because it can condition another moment later on and thus right understanding can grow.”

Its condition. “The condition for right mindfulness is intellectual13 understanding of what nama and rūpa are: realities which appear through the six doorways.” That is what this course has been for. “When we read in the Buddhist scriptures14 time and again about the realities which appear through the six doors or we listen to talks about nama and rūpa, and we understand what we read or what we hear, then the intellectual understanding can condition the arising of mindfulness. Even one moment of mindfulness is valuable because it can condition another moment later on and thus right understanding can grow.” The essay calls this “the highest form of wholesomeness”, because “it is the only way to eradicate15 attachment16, aversion17 and ignorance18“.

What it is not. Many people think that mindfulness means doing everything slowly and carefully, with attention to what the hands and feet are doing. The essay says this is not it. “When one believes that one does all one’s actions in a day with thoughtfulness but there is no awareness19 of nama and rūpa, it is not the development of insight. When one, for example, follows what one’s hands and feet are doing in a day one does not learn anything about nama and rūpa, about what is real, about impermanence20.” Hands and feet are concepts21. What is real when the hand moves is hardness, motion, the body-consciousness that experiences them, and the citta (consciousness) that moves them.

Doing everything as usual. “In the development of insight we do everything as usual, but in our daily life there can be mindfulness of a nama or a rūpa, a moment of ‘study with mindfulness’, study through the practice.” The essay gives an example from its author’s own life:

“When my husband takes my hand, there is, as we say, a ‘human contact’. What are the realities? There is attachment and this is real, we do not have to try to suppress it. There can, in a very natural way, be study with mindfulness of a nama or a rūpa. What appears through the body-sense22? Not a person, not my husband. Heat or cold, hardness or softness can appear through the body-sense. We do not have to think about it, it can be directly experienced. Through mindfulness we can prove that no person is experienced through the body-sense, that a person does not exist. There is no person, only different namas and rupas appearing one at a time, and they do not stay.”

The essay does not say that the attachment is wrong and must be stopped. “There is attachment and this is real, we do not have to try to suppress it.” The practice is not to change what arises, but to know it. And: “Clinging23 to people brings sorrow; eventually I will have to take leave from my husband, nothing is permanent.”

Kamma, again. With more understanding, “we will have a different view of the events of our life. We like to make plans but often things do not happen the way we would like them to. Our good and bad deeds24 (kamma) are the causes in our life which bring their results25 in the form of pleasant and unpleasant experiences. When we understand that our life is nama and rūpa which arise because of their own conditions, not because of our will, we will be less attached to pleasant results and less inclined26 to blame others for unpleasant things we experience. There are only nama and rūpa and we are not master of them.”

For others too. The essay’s last sentences answer the question it began with. “Through the development of insight we will become more patient, we will have more loving-kindness27 and compassion28. Thus, the development of insight is to the benefit of other people as well.”

The goal. The appendix to the book, after listing all the conditioned29 realities, ends with the one that is not conditioned. “There is one type of unconditioned30 reality and that is called nibbāna (in Sanskrit, nirvana). Nibbāna is described as the ‘deathless31‘, the ‘cool’, the ‘incomparable’, the ‘peaceful’. It is the end of craving32, the goal of the Buddha’s teachings.” Lesson 2 said that nibbāna (the end of all troubles) cannot be understood by reading about it. But the road to it begins with hearing what nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter33) are, goes on with understanding what has been heard, and continues, one short moment at a time, with sati (mindfulness) of the reality that is appearing right now.

1. King Pasenadi asked the Buddha how many kinds of things make for trouble, suffering and distress. What was the answer? (a) one: ignorance (b) three: greed, hate and delusion (c) ten: the ten fetters (d) eighty-nine 2. Who or what can eradicate defilements, according to the essay? 3. What does the essay say character really is? (a) a lasting thing in a person (b) an accumulation of experiences handed on from each moment of consciousness to the next (c) the body (d) the result of kamma only 6. (a) sitting very still (b) intellectual understanding of what nāma and rūpa are (c) following what the hands and feet are doing (d) wanting it strongly 10. (a) the deathless, the cool, the incomparable, the peaceful (b) the high, the far, the bright, the wide (c) earth, water, fire and wind (d) seeing, hearing, smelling and tasting

Going on from here. The preface to the book says: “We should apply ourselves to the study of all parts of

the Buddha’s teaching contained in the Pāḷi Canon-to the Vinaya (the books of discipline for the Sangha),

to the Suttas (the books of discourses) and to the Abhidhamma. Our own clarification of the teachings

through reading, wise consideration and contemplation will be of much benefit to us and to all others who

come into contact with us.” The book’s own reading list begins with Abhidhamma in Daily Life by Nina

van Gorkom, which takes each of these lists further and can be read free of charge on abhidhamma.org.

After that comes the Abhidhammattha Saṅgaha (the Compendium of Abhidhamma), the short manual by

the Elder Anuruddha that every student of the Abhidhamma in Burma, Sri Lanka and Thailand has learnt

for a thousand years, and which gives all the lists in this course in full.

Hard words

Every hard English word in this book has a small number after it the first time it is met in a chapter, and its meaning is given at the end of that chapter. Here are all of them together, in alphabetical order.

absolute: complete and real in itself; not depending on names or ideas abstain: to hold back from doing something, such as lying abuse: to treat or speak to someone cruelly and rudely accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it adaptability: being able to fit to what is needed adverting: turning towards something aggregate: a group or heap of things taken together alms: food given to monks alteration: a change amity: friendliness analyse: to take something apart carefully to see what it is made of arise: to come up; to begin; to happen ascetic: a person who gives up home and comfort to live simply and seek the truth; or that hard way of living atrocious: very cruel and terrible attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being bodysense: the sense of touch, all over the body bough: a big branch of a tree canon: the set of writings accepted as the true teaching cessation: stopping; coming to an end characteristic: the mark by which something is known; what is special about it chariot: a cart with two wheels pulled by horses, used in old times for war and travel chronicle: a history written down in order of time classification: sorting things into kinds clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go cohesion: holding together; the sticking-together of the parts commentary: an old explanation of a text, written to make it clear compassion: wanting to help someone who is suffering composure: calmness conceit: thinking oneself better than others, or worse, or just as good; pride that compares concentration: keeping the mind on one thing

Where it comes from

This course follows An Introduction to the Abhidhamma, printed for free distribution by the Dhamma Study Group, Bangkok, at New Year 1980, and dedicated to Sister Sudhammā (Pauline Ofner, 1927 to 1979). The book has two essays and an appendix. The first essay, Abhidhamma Notes by Jill Jordan and Richard Giles, was written as an introduction to the Abhidhamma for a comparative religion class in Adelaide, South Australia; Lessons 1 to 10 keep to its order, its explanations and, as far as a course for young readers allows, its words. The second essay, Abhidhamma and Practice by Nina van Gorkom, was written for a Dhamma publication in Holland; Lessons 11 and 12 follow it. The appendix, The Paramattha Dhammas, lists all 89 (or 121) kinds of consciousness, the 52 mental factors and the 28 kinds of matter, and the tables in Lessons 3, 4 and 5 are taken from it. Where this course quotes a sentence in quotation marks, the words are those of the book or of the translation it uses.

The book itself draws on these ancient texts, and the course has gone to them for the stories:

The Atthasālinī (The Expositor), Buddhaghosa’s commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the first book of the Abhidhamma, for the teaching of the Abhidhamma in Tāvatiṃsa (the heaven of the Thirtythree), the created Buddha, Sāriputta and his five hundred pupils, and the recital of the Abhidhamma at the First Council. The Dhammapada commentary, for the descent from heaven at Saṅkassa. The Mahāvaṃsa (the Great Chronicle of Ceylon), chapters 14 and 33, in the translation of Wilhelm Geiger, for the Elder Mahinda’s meeting with King Devānampiyatissa and for the writing down of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) in Sri Lanka. The Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya (discipline), for the three councils. The Visuddhimagga (the Path of Purity) by Buddhaghosa, for the chariot and for the closing verse, both quoted in the book. The Saṃyutta Nikāya (the Grouped Discourses): the discourse on the heap of sticks (ii, 178) and King Pasenadi’s question about the three things that make for trouble (the Kindred Sayings, I, III, iii, 3), both quoted in the book; the verses of the nun Vajirā (the Vajirā Sutta), the discourse on the dirt on the fingernail and the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, in the translation of Bhikkhu Sujato. The Udāna (the Inspired Utterances), for the Buddha’s words to Bāhiya, in the translation of Bhikkhu Sujato. The Majjhima Nikāya (the Middle Length Discourses), the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, for the elements in the body. The Dhammapada, verse 100, quoted at the front of the book. The Abhidhammattha Saṅgaha (the Compendium of Abhidhamma) by the Elder Anuruddha, for the Pāḷi names of the ten bad deeds, the ten bases of merit, the planes, the fetters and the moments of a sense-door process, where the book gives only the English or does not go into them.

Where the ancient texts and modern scholars differ, this course follows the ancient texts. In particular, it follows the Atthasālinī (The Expositor) in holding that the Abhidhamma is the Buddha’s own teaching, recited at the First Council, and that the Kathāvatthu (Points of Controversy) was set out by the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa at the Third Council on an outline the Buddha had laid down.

Answers

Quiz 1 (lessons 1 and 2) 1. (b) “higher” and “reality” or “truth”. The book says: “‘abhi’ meaning ‘higher’ or ‘greater’ and ‘dhamma’ which means ‘reality’ or ‘truth’”. So Abhidhamma means “the higher truth” or “the higher teaching”. 2. (b) seven; the Paṭṭhāna. There are seven books. The Paṭṭhāna (the book of conditions) is “the largest and the most important Abhidhamma work”. 3. In Tāvatiṃsa (the heaven of the Thirty-three), to his mother and the devas (heavenly beings), for the three months of the rainy season in the seventh year after his enlightenment. 4. Each day, when the Buddha came down to the lake Anotatta, he told Sāriputta the method of what had been taught in heaven that day. Sāriputta taught it to his five hundred pupils, who memorised and mastered it. 5. (b) a stag, which was a deva (heavenly being) in disguise. The king was hunting on the Missaka mountain. A deva (heavenly being) appeared “in the form of an elk-stag browsing in the thicket”, and “the stag in his flight drew near to the thera”. 6. To find out whether the king was quick enough to follow the teaching. When the king answered well, “Thou hast a shrewd wit, O ruler of men!” Only when he knew the king was keen-witted did he preach. 7. False. For a long time nothing was written down; the whole canon was committed to memory by groups of monks. It was written on palm leaves in Sri Lanka more than four hundred years after the Buddha, “in order that the true doctrine might endure”. 8. (b) the sound of the bell. Sound is an object of experience, and “does not experience anything (this being the characteristic of rūpa)”. Hearing, liking and remembering all experience something, so they are nāma (mind). 9. Citta (consciousness), cetasika (mental factors), rūpa (matter) and nibbāna (the end of all troubles). Nibbāna is the one unconditioned reality: “there are no causes which make it arise”. 10. False. The book says: “Seeing is not hearing. They do not occur together, they occur at different moments, although we are under the impression that they do occur together.” 11. It “is not matter, it is not a place where one goes, it has no form or shape or solidity, it is not something that one unites with”. It does not begin or end, and it cannot be understood intellectually.

Quiz 2 (lessons 3 and 4) 1. (b) 89 kinds in 4 classes. “Citta (consciousness) is of 89 different types. Cittas are divided into four categories”: kusala (good) 21, akusala (bad) 12, vipāka (result) 36 and kiriya (functional) 20. 2. 1. akusala citta (bad consciousness), 12; 2. kiriya citta (functional consciousness), 20; 3. kusala citta (good consciousness), 21; 4. vipāka citta (result consciousness), 36. 12 bad, 20 functional, 21 good, 36 result. Together they make 89.

3. (a) being bored. The book’s examples are “when we get angry, when we are bored, when we are depressed, when we are absorbed in beautiful things, when we kill or steal or lie to people or when we are restless”. Bowing and holding back from a lie are kusala (good). Seeing a colour is vipāka (result).
